questions.q: What is the main purpose of a VLAN?
choices: Split one switch into separate Layer 2 broadcast domains
Increase the speed of switch ports
questions.explain: Each VLAN is its own broadcast domain (and usually its own IP subnet). Traffic between VLANs needs a router or Layer 3 switch.

questions.q: Which IEEE standard tags Ethernet frames with a VLAN ID on trunk links?
questions.explain: 802.1Q inserts a 4-byte tag containing a 12-bit VLAN ID. 802.1D = STP, 802.3ad = LACP, 802.11 = Wi-Fi.

questions.q: How large is the 802.1Q tag inserted into an Ethernet frame?
questions.explain: The tag is 4 bytes (32 bits): TPID 0x8100, plus 3-bit priority (CoS), 1-bit DEI and the 12-bit VLAN ID. The VLAN ID itself is 12 bits.

questions.q: How are frames in the NATIVE VLAN sent across an 802.1Q trunk?
questions.explain: Native VLAN traffic crosses the trunk untagged. Both ends must agree on the native VLAN, or traffic leaks between VLANs (and CDP warns of a mismatch).

questions.q: What is the default native VLAN (and default VLAN) on Cisco switches?
questions.explain: VLAN 1. Best practice: move the native VLAN to an unused VLAN and don't put users in VLAN 1, to reduce VLAN-hopping risk.

questions.q: An ACCESS port carries traffic for how many data VLANs?
questions.explain: Access ports belong to a single data VLAN (optionally plus a voice VLAN). Trunk ports carry multiple VLANs using 802.1Q tags.

questions.q: Why does Spanning Tree Protocol exist?
choices: To prevent Layer 2 loops when there are redundant links
questions.explain: Ethernet frames have no TTL, so a loop causes broadcast storms and MAC table instability. STP blocks redundant paths until they're needed.

questions.q: How is the STP root bridge elected?
choices: Lowest bridge ID (priority, then MAC address)
questions.explain: Lowest bridge ID wins. Bridge ID = priority (default 32768 + VLAN ID) followed by MAC address. Lower the priority to choose your root deliberately.

questions.q: What is the default STP bridge priority on a switch (before the VLAN ID is added)?
questions.explain: Default priority is 32768. With PVST+ the extended system ID adds the VLAN number, so VLAN 10 shows 32778. Priorities go in steps of 4096.

questions.q: On a non-root switch, the port with the lowest-cost path to the root bridge becomes the:
questions.explain: Each non-root switch has ONE root port (best path to root). Each segment has one designated port. Others become alternate/backup and block.

questions.q: Order the classic 802.1D STP port states a port moves through on the way to forwarding.
questions.explain: Blocking (20s max age) → Listening (15s) → Learning (15s, building the MAC table) → Forwarding. That's why classic STP takes 30–50 seconds. RSTP is much faster.

questions.q: Which IEEE standard defines Rapid Spanning Tree (RSTP)?
questions.explain: 802.1w = RSTP. 802.1D = original STP, 802.1s = MSTP, 802.1X = port-based authentication.

questions.q: What does PortFast do?
choices: Moves an access port straight to forwarding, skipping listening/learning
Turns the port into a trunk
Disables STP on the whole switch
questions.explain: PortFast is for ports to end hosts, so a PC gets connectivity (and DHCP) immediately. Never use it on links to other switches.

questions.q: A PortFast port with BPDU Guard enabled receives a BPDU. What happens?
questions.explain: A BPDU on an edge port means someone plugged in a switch. BPDU Guard err-disables the port to protect the topology.

questions.q: What is the default administrative distance of OSPF?
questions.explain: Connected 0, static 1, eBGP 20, EIGRP 90, OSPF 110, IS-IS 115, RIP 120, iBGP 200.

questions.q: Which route source is MOST trusted (lowest administrative distance)?
questions.explain: Connected routes have AD 0; static routes have AD 1. Lower AD = more trustworthy.

questions.q: A router has routes to 10.1.0.0/16 and 10.1.1.0/24. Which does it use for a packet to 10.1.1.5?
questions.explain: Longest prefix match always comes first: the most specific route wins, no matter the AD or metric.

questions.q: OSPF and EIGRP both offer a route to 172.16.5.0/24. Which one goes in the routing table?
choices: The one with the lower metric
questions.explain: With identical prefixes from different sources, the lowest administrative distance wins. Metrics are only compared within the same protocol.

questions.q: What metric does OSPF use?
questions.explain: OSPF cost = reference bandwidth (100 Mbps default) ÷ interface bandwidth. RIP uses hop count; EIGRP uses bandwidth + delay; BGP uses path attributes.

questions.q: What is the OSPF backbone area?
questions.explain: Area 0 (0.0.0.0) is the backbone. In multi-area OSPF, every other area must connect to Area 0.

questions.q: How does a Cisco router choose its OSPF router ID?
choices: Manual router-id → highest loopback IP → highest active interface IP
questions.explain: 1) router-id command, 2) highest IP on an up loopback, 3) highest IP on an up physical interface. Set it manually for stability.

questions.q: Which multicast address does OSPF use to reach ALL OSPF routers?
On a broadcast segment, how is the OSPF Designated Router (DR) elected?
choices: Highest OSPF interface priority, then highest router ID
questions.explain: Highest priority (default 1) wins; ties go to the highest router ID. Priority 0 means never become DR. Elections are non-preemptive.

questions.q: How is an IPv4 default route written?
questions.explain: 0.0.0.0/0 matches every destination with the shortest possible prefix, so it's used only when nothing more specific matches. It's the 'gateway of last resort'.

questions.q: What is a floating static route?
choices: A static route with a higher AD, used as a backup when the primary route disappears
A route that moves between interfaces
A default route learned via DHCP
A route with no next hop
questions.explain: Give a static route an AD higher than the dynamic protocol (e.g. `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 10.9.9.1 200`) and it only appears if the primary route is lost.

questions.q: OSPF is what kind of routing protocol?
questions.explain: OSPF routers flood LSAs, build an identical link-state database and run Dijkstra's SPF algorithm. RIP is distance-vector; BGP is path-vector.

questions.q: What is RIP's maximum hop count?
questions.explain: RIP considers 16 hops infinite, so it's limited to small networks.

questions.q: Which EtherChannel negotiation protocol is the IEEE open standard?
questions.explain: LACP (802.3ad / 802.1AX) is open; PAgP is Cisco-proprietary. EtherChannel bundles links so STP treats them as one.

questions.q: What problem do First Hop Redundancy Protocols (HSRP, VRRP, GLBP) solve?
choices: They provide a backup default gateway via a shared virtual IP
questions.explain: Hosts point at a virtual gateway IP/MAC shared by two or more routers. If the active router dies, the standby takes over seamlessly.

questions.q: Which First Hop Redundancy Protocol is an open (IETF) standard?
questions.explain: VRRP is the IETF standard (RFC 5798). HSRP and GLBP are Cisco-proprietary.

questions.q: In 'router-on-a-stick', how does one physical router interface route between VLANs?
choices: Subinterfaces, each with 802.1Q encapsulation and an IP for one VLAN
questions.explain: e.g. `interface g0/0.10` + `encapsulation dot1Q 10` + `ip address 10.0.10.1 255.255.255.0`. The switch port facing the router is a trunk.

questions.q: A Layer 3 switch routes between VLANs using:
choices: SVIs (interface vlan X) with IP addresses
A separate router for each VLAN
questions.explain: Switched Virtual Interfaces act as each VLAN's default gateway. Enable `ip routing` on the switch.

questions.q: Which neighbor discovery protocol is vendor-neutral?
questions.explain: LLDP (802.1AB) works across vendors. CDP is Cisco-proprietary (and enabled by default on Cisco gear).

questions.q: In `show ip route` output, what does the code **O** mean?
questions.explain: C = connected, L = local (the router's own /32), S = static, O = OSPF, D = EIGRP, R = RIP, B = BGP, * = candidate default.

questions.q: What is the default administrative distance of a static route?
questions.explain: Static = 1 (connected = 0). Static routes are trusted over any dynamic protocol unless you raise their AD (floating static).

questions.q: What is the highest usable VLAN ID?
questions.explain: 12-bit VLAN ID = 0–4095, with 0 and 4095 reserved, so 1–4094 are usable. 1–1005 is normal range; 1006–4094 is extended.

questions.q: Order these route sources from MOST trusted (lowest AD) to LEAST trusted.
questions.explain: Memorize: 0, 1, 20, 90, 110, 120. (iBGP is 200, and 255 means 'never use this route'.)

questions.q: Order the criteria a router uses to pick a route, from FIRST checked to LAST.
questions.explain: Most specific prefix first. If two sources offer the same prefix, lowest AD wins. Within one protocol, lowest metric wins (ties may load-balance).

questions.q: Order the OSPF neighbor states from first to FULL adjacency.
questions.explain: Hello seen (Init) → bidirectional (2-Way, DR election) → master/slave chosen (ExStart) → DBDs swapped (Exchange) → LSRs/LSUs (Loading) → Full.

questions.q: Order what a router does when forwarding an IP packet.
items: Receive the frame and strip the Layer 2 header
Look up the destination IP (longest prefix match)
Decrement TTL and update the header checksum
Build a new Layer 2 frame for the next hop and send it
questions.explain: IP addresses stay the same end to end (ignoring NAT), but the Layer 2 frame is rebuilt at every hop with new source/destination MACs.

questions.q: Display R1's IPv4 routing table.
questions.output:
Gateway of last resort is 203.0.113.1 to network 0.0.0.0
S*    0.0.0.0/0 [1/0] via 203.0.113.1
      10.0.0.0/8 is variably subnetted, 4 subnets, 2 masks
C        10.1.1.0/24 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
L        10.1.1.1/32 is directly connected, GigabitEthernet0/0
O        10.2.2.0/24 [110/2] via 10.1.12.2, 00:04:12, GigabitEthernet0/1
questions.explain: `show ip route` (abbreviated `sh ip ro`). [110/2] means AD 110 / metric 2.

questions.q: Show a one-line summary of every interface with its IP address and up/down status.
questions.output:
Interface              IP-Address      OK? Method Status                Protocol
GigabitEthernet0/0     10.1.1.1        YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/1     10.1.12.1       YES manual up                    up
GigabitEthernet0/2     unassigned      YES unset  administratively down down
questions.explain: `show ip interface brief` (`sh ip int br`) is the #1 troubleshooting command. 'administratively down' means someone typed `shutdown`.

questions.q: Display the switch's MAC address table.
questions.explain: `show mac address-table` shows learned MACs per VLAN and port. Older IOS used `show mac-address-table`.

questions.q: List the VLANs on this switch and which access ports belong to each.
questions.output:
VLAN Name                             Status    Ports
---- -------------------------------- --------- ------------------
1    default                          active    Gi0/2, Gi0/4
10   SALES                            active    Gi0/3, Gi0/6
20   ENGINEERING                      active    Gi0/5
questions.explain: `show vlan brief` lists VLANs and their ACCESS ports. Trunk ports don't appear here; use `show interfaces trunk`.

questions.q: Enter global configuration mode.
questions.output:
Enter configuration commands, one per line.  End with CNTL/Z.
R1(config)#
questions.explain: `configure terminal` (`conf t`) moves from privileged EXEC (#) to global config ((config)#). Use `end` or Ctrl+Z to leave.

questions.q: Configure a static DEFAULT route pointing to next hop 203.0.113.1.
questions.explain: `ip route 0.0.0.0 0.0.0.0 <next-hop>` sends anything without a more specific match to the ISP. IOS uses dotted masks here, not /0.

questions.q: Verify which OSPF neighbors R1 has formed adjacencies with.
questions.output:
Neighbor ID     Pri   State           Dead Time   Address         Interface
2.2.2.2           1   FULL/DR         00:00:35    10.1.12.2       Gi0/1
3.3.3.3           1   FULL/BDR        00:00:31    10.1.12.3       Gi0/1
questions.explain: FULL means the databases are synchronized. Stuck in INIT or EXSTART usually means mismatched timers, area, subnet, authentication or MTU.

questions.q: Show the spanning tree status (root bridge, port roles and states).
questions.output:
VLAN0010
  Spanning tree enabled protocol rstp
  Root ID    Priority    24586
             Address     0011.2233.4455
  Bridge ID  Priority    32778
Interface   Role Sts Cost  Prio.Nbr Type

Gi0/2       Altn BLK 4     128.2    P2p
questions.explain: `show spanning-tree` shows the root, your bridge ID and each port's role (Root/Desg/Altn) and state (FWD/BLK).

questions.q: This interface is already an access port. Assign it to VLAN 10.
questions.explain: `switchport mode access` + `switchport access vlan 10`. If VLAN 10 doesn't exist yet, the switch creates it.

questions.q: Statically make this interface an 802.1Q trunk.
questions.output:
SW1(config-if)#
%LINEPROTO-5-UPDOWN: Line protocol on Interface Gi0/24, changed state to up
questions.explain: `switchport mode trunk`. Hard-code trunks rather than relying on DTP, and consider `switchport nonegotiate`.

questions.q: Save the running configuration so it survives a reboot.
questions.explain: The running-config lives in RAM; startup-config lives in NVRAM. `copy run start` (or the classic `wr`) saves it.

questions.q: Enable OSPF area 0 on all interfaces in 10.0.0.0/24 using a network statement.
questions.output:
R1(config-router)#
%OSPF-5-ADJCHG: Process 1, Nbr 2.2.2.2 on Gi0/1 from LOADING to FULL
questions.explain: OSPF network statements use a WILDCARD mask (inverse of the subnet mask): /24 → 0.0.0.255. You could also use `ip ospf 1 area 0` on the interface.

questions.q: What is the 'gateway of last resort'?
choices: The default route used when no more specific route matches
questions.explain: It's the next hop for the default route (0.0.0.0/0). Without one, packets to unknown networks are dropped.

questions.q: In which VLAN-hopping attack does an attacker send frames carrying two 802.1Q tags?
choices: Double tagging, which exploits the native VLAN
questions.explain: The first switch strips the outer (native VLAN) tag and forwards the frame, still tagged for the victim VLAN, across the trunk. Fix: use an unused native VLAN, or tag the native VLAN.
